## ABSTRACT

BACKGROUND Safe and effective decongestion remains an important therapeutic goal in patients hospitalized for

heart failure.

OBJECTIVES The authors evaluated the effect of dapagliflozin on multiple clinically relevant measures of congestion

among patients hospitalized for heart failure.

METHODS This was a prespecified analysis of DAPA ACT HF-TIMI 68 (Dapagliflozin Effect on Cardiovascular Events in

Acute Heart Failure—Thrombolysis in Myocardial Infarction 68), a randomized, placebo-controlled trial evaluating in-

hospital initiation of dapagliflozin on clinical outcomes through 2 months. The authors assessed placebo-adjusted

changes from baseline in modified EVEREST (Efficacy of Vasopressin Antagonism in Heart Failure) Composite Congestion

Score (CCS), body weight, mean daily loop diuretic dose (furosemide 40 mg intravenous [IV] equivalents), and body

weight adjusted for mean daily loop diuretic dose (diuretic efficiency) at 1 week, 1 month, and 2 months using linear

mixed-effects models for repeated measures.

RESULTS At randomization, 12%, 63%, and 24% had no congestion (CCS 0), mild-to-moderate congestion (CCS 1-3),

and severe congestion (CCS 4-9), respectively. Compared with placebo, dapagliflozin improved all decongestion-related

endpoints by 1 week, including CCS (least squares mean difference [LSMD]: − 0.18; 95% CI: − 0.33 to − 0.04; P = 0.011),

body weight (LSMD: − 0.60 kg; 95% CI: − 0.95 to − 0.26; P < 0.001), mean daily loop diuretic dose (LSMD: − 0.12

furosemide 40-mg IV equivalents; 95% CI: − 0.22 to − 0.02; P = 0.014), and diuretic efficiency (LSMD: − 0.93 kg/

furosemide 40 mg IV equivalents; 95% CI: − 1.61 to − 0.25; P = 0.008). These improvements were sustained through

2 months, with progressive increases in diuretic efficiency through 2 months (LSMD: − 1.99 kg/furosemide 40 mg IV

equivalents; 95% CI: − 3.19 to − 0.78; P < 0.001).

CONCLUSIONS In-hospital initiation of dapagliflozin led to modest but significant improvements across multiple mea-

sures of congestion within 1 week that were sustained through 2 months. Diuretic efficiency progressively improved through

## H

eart failure (HF) hospitalizations

are associated with a high risk of

death and other adverse outcomes

during hospital admission and in the early

postdischarge period, with congestion

serving as a key pathophysiological and

clinical feature. 1 Despite the use of loop di-

uretics, residual congestion at discharge is

common and strongly associated with HF

readmission and mortality. These observa-

tions have motivated interest in therapies

that more effectively promote decongestion

during hospitalization and in the early post-

discharge period. 2-5

Sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 (SGLT2) in-

hibitors, such as dapagliflozin, are a foundational

component of guideline-directed pharmacological

therapy for HF across the spectrum of left ventricular

ejection fraction (LVEF), with randomized trials

demonstrating robust reductions in the risk of wors-

ening heart failure (WHF) and cardiovascular death

(CVD) in ambulatory patients with HF. 6,7 In addition,

the totality of randomized trial data suggests that in-

hospital initiation of SGLT2 inhibitors reduces the

early risk of CVD or WHF and of all-cause mortality in

the early postdischarge period in hospitalized pa-

tients with HF. 8,9 Beyond their established clinical

benefits, SGLT2 inhibitors may have favorable early

effects on fluid balance through mechanisms that

include osmotic diuresis, natriuresis, and facilitation

of interstitial drainage. 10 These effects may be

particularly advantageous in the management of

decompensated HF, uniquely positioning SGLT2 in-

hibitors to achieve the dual goals of effective decon-

gestion and durable cardiovascular risk reduction.

Despite the theoretical benefits of SGLT2 inhibitors

on decongestion, studies evaluating the impact of

in-hospital initiation of SGLT2 inhibitors on

decongestion-related endpoints have produced

mixed results. 11-13 DAPA ACT HF-TIMI 68 (Dapagli-

flozin Effect on Cardiovascular Events in Acute Heart

Failure-Thrombolysis in Myocardial Infarction 68;

NCT04363697) was a randomized, placebo-controlled

trial evaluating in-hospital initiation of dapagliflozin

on clinical outcomes through 2 months in patients

hospitalized with a primary diagnosis of HF. 8 In this

prespecified secondary analysis of DAPA ACT HF-

TIMI 68, we evaluated the effect of in-hospital initi-

ation of dapagliflozin on multiple decongestion-

related endpoints in the early postdischarge period.

## METHODS

STUDY POPULATION. The DAPA ACT HF-TIMI 68

trial design, baseline characteristics, and main

results have previously been published. 8,14 In brief,

DAPA ACT HF-TIMI 68 was a randomized, double-

blind, placebo-controlled trial evaluating the

efficacy and safety of in-hospital initiation of dapa-

gliflozin in 2,401 patients hospitalized for HF.

Eligible patients were at least 18 years old and had a

primary diagnosis of HF, including signs and symp-

toms of fluid overload with elevated natriuretic

peptide levels. Randomization occurred during the

index hospitalization, at least 24 hours and no later

than 14 days after hospital admission, and as early as

possible after initial clinical stabilization. Stabiliza-

tion criteria included no intensification in the dose of

intravenous (IV) diuretics during the 12 hours before

randomization and no use of IV vasodilators or ino-

tropes during the 24 hours before randomization.

Patients were randomized in a 1:1 ratio to receive

dapagliflozin (10 mg once daily) or matching placebo

and were followed for clinical outcomes through

2 months. The trial protocol was approved by the

institutional review board or ethics committee at

each participating site and all participants provided

written informed consent before enrollment.

DECONGESTION-RELATED ENDPOINTS. The primary

decongestion-related endpoint for this analysis was

the placebo-adjusted change from baseline in modi-

fied EVEREST (Efficacy of Vasopressin Antagonism in

Heart Failure) Composite Congestion Score (CCS). 2

Six HF signs and symptoms—orthopnea, peripheral

edema, jugular venous pressure (JVP), rales, fatigue,

and dyspnea—were graded on a scale from 0 (absent)

to 3 (severe) at randomization, 1 week, 1 month, and

2 months. Modified CCS was calculated by summing

the individual component scores for orthopnea, pe-

ripheral edema, and JVP (maximum score = 9 points).

In the prespecified primary analysis, placebo-

adjusted change from baseline in CCS was analyzed

using a complete-case approach, restricting to pa-

tients with evaluable scores (ie, available scores for

all 3 CCS components) at both baseline and the rele-

vant follow-up visit. Sensitivity analyses were per-

formed using multiple imputation methods to handle

missing CCS data. In addition, placebo-adjusted

change from baseline was assessed for each individ-

ual HF sign and symptom. Full details are provided in

the Supplemental Methods.

Other decongestion-related endpoints included

placebo-adjusted change from baseline in body

weight, placebo-adjusted change from baseline in

mean daily loop diuretic dose (expressed as furose-

mide 40 mg IV equivalents), and placebo-adjusted

change from baseline in body weight adjusted for

mean daily loop diuretic dose, with greater weight loss

per unit of loop diuretic defining greater diuretic effi-

ciency. Analyses of body weight and diuretic effi-

ciency excluded observations of change in body

weight below the first and above the 99th percentiles

to mitigate against the impact of extreme outliers.

Loop diuretic equivalence is shown in the

Supplemental Methods. Analysis of these endpoints

was similarly restricted to patients with evaluable data

at both baseline and the relevant follow-up visit. No

imputation methods were used for these endpoints.

CLINICAL ENDPOINTS. The primary clinical endpoint

in DAPA ACT HF-TIMI 68 was the composite of CVD/

WHF through 2 months. A WHF event was defined as:

1) worsening of signs or symptoms of HF during the

index hospitalization, resulting in treatment with IV

inotropes, mechanical circulatory support, invasive

ventilatory support, or heart transplantation; 2) un-

planned rehospitalization for HF; or 3) urgent

ambulatory HF visit resulting in treatment with IV

diuretic therapy. Secondary clinical endpoints

included each individual component of the primary

clinical endpoint, cardiovascular death or rehospi-

talization for HF, and all-cause death.

STATISTICAL ANALYSES. Patients were classified as

having no congestion (CCS 0), mild-to-moderate

congestion (CCS 1-3), or severe congestion (CCS 4-9)

at the time of randomization. The threshold between

mild-to-moderate and severe congestion was derived

based on maximizing the Youden index applied to a

time-dependent receiver operating characteristic

curve at 60 days postrandomization for the primary

clinical endpoint because there are no well-

established thresholds for assessing severity of re-

sidual congestion during HF hospitalization rather

than at the time of discharge. 15,16 Baseline charac-

teristics were summarized according to baseline

congestion severity using counts and percentages for

categorical variables and medians (Q1-Q3) for

continuous variables. Trends across congestion strata

were assessed using the Jonckheere-Terpstra test for

ordinal and continuous variables and the Cochran-

Armitage trend test for binary variables.

The associations of congestion parameters at

randomization, including CCS and individual HF

signs and symptoms, with time-to-event clinical

endpoints were evaluated using multivariable Cox

proportional hazards models adjusted for age, esti-

mated glomerular filtration rate, LVEF, previous HF

hospitalization, previous stroke, atrial fibrillation,

use of invasive or noninvasive ventilation before

randomization, and randomized treatment. Adjusted

HRs (aHRs) and corresponding 95% CIs were esti-

mated per 2-point increase in CCS (corresponding

approximately to 1 SD). P values (Wald test) were

obtained from the Cox model. The proportional

hazards assumption was confirmed using scaled

Schoenfeld residual plots. Owing to inconclusive

evidence regarding the linearity assumption for the

relationship between CCS and the log-hazard for the

primary clinical endpoint, aHRs also were estimated

for CCS categories with uncongested (CCS = 0) as the

reference group. Firth’s correction was used when a

congestion category did not have any events for a

given endpoint. Adjusted cumulative risk curves for

time-to-event clinical endpoints by CCS category

were derived from a multivariable Cox model using

direct standardization to the covariate distribution in

our cohort with evaluable CCS.

The effect of dapagliflozin on changes in CCS over

time was analyzed using a linear mixed model for

repeated measures, including all eligible postbase-

line visits, with fixed effects for baseline CCS,

randomization stratification factors (HF chronicity

and type 2 diabetes), randomized treatment assign-

ment (dapagliflozin or placebo), visit (week 1, month

1, and month 2), and interaction of treatment and

visit with an unstructured covariance matrix to

## RESULTS

DISTRIBUTION OF BASELINE CONGESTION

PARAMETERS. Among 2,401 randomized trial par-

ticipants, 1,676 patients had complete baseline CCS

data and were included in the primary CCS analyses.

Baseline characteristics of patients with vs without

complete baseline CCS data are shown in

Supplemental Table 1. Among patients with complete

baseline CCS data, complete follow-up CCS data were

available in 1,154 (68.9%) at week 1, 1,253 (74.8%) at

month 1, and 1,165 (69.5%) at month 2. At randomi-

zation, the median CCS was 2 (Q1-Q3: 1-3), with

12.2%, 63.3%, and 24.5% classified as uncongested

(CCS 0), mild-to-moderately congested (CCS 1-3), and

severely congested (CCS 4-9), respectively. Irre-

spective of randomized treatment, CCS scores tended

to decrease over time, with median CCS scores of

2 (Q1-Q3: 1-3), 1 (Q1-Q3: 1-2), 1 (Q1-Q3: 0-2), and 1

(Q1-Q3: 0-1) at randomization, week 1, month 1, and

month 2, respectively (Supplemental Table 2,

Supplemental Figure 1).

BASELINE CHARACTERISTICS OF STUDY

POPULATION. Baseline characteristics are presented

by baseline CCS in Table 1. Age, sex, and LVEF were

similar across congestion categories. Patients in

higher congestion categories were more likely to be

Black, and to have a higher body mass index, type 2

diabetes mellitus, and estimated glomerular filtration

rate <60 mL/min/1.73 m 2 . Patients in higher conges-

tion categories were also more likely to have chronic

HF and at least 1 previous HF hospitalization. Greater

congestion severity was associated with lower Kan-

sas City Cardiomyopathy Questionnaire scores

(reflecting poorer health status) and higher natri-

uretic peptide levels. Median baseline body weight

was 82.0 kg (Q1-Q3: 69.0-96.7 kg), 84.4 kg (Q1-Q3:

71.1-101.6 kg), and 96.2 kg (Q1-Q3: 79.1-113.7 kg)

among patients with CCS 0, CCS 1 to 3, and CCS 4 to

9, respectively.

PROGNOSTIC SIGNIFICANCE OF CONGESTION

VARIABLES AND EVEREST CCS. Event rates

increased in a graded fashion across increasing

congestion categories for all primary and secondary

clinical endpoints (Figure 1). Baseline congestion

severity was independently associated with pro-

gressively higher risk of each clinical endpoint

through 2 months (Figure 2). For the primary clinical

endpoint of CVD or WHF, aHRs increased from 1.97

(95% CI: 1.12-3.49) for CCS 1-3 to 2.23 (95% CI: 1.22-

4.07) for CCS 4-9 compared with CCS 0. A similar

gradient was observed for all-cause death (aHR: 1.95;

95% CI: 0.59-6.39 and aHR: 3.60; 95% CI: 1.08-12.0,

respectively). Baseline congestion severity did not

appear to modify the effect of dapagliflozin on clin-

ical outcomes (Supplemental Figure 2).

Among individual HF signs and symptoms, in

adjusted analyses, severity of peripheral edema was

independently associated with the risks of both CVD

or WHF (P trend = 0.008) and all-cause death

(P trend < 0.001). Severity of JVP elevation was

independently associated with risk of all-cause death

(P trend = 0.027), and severity of orthopnea was

independently associated with risk of CVD or WHF

(P trend = 0.010). By contrast, severity of dyspnea,

fatigue, and rales was not independently associated

with either of these short-term morbidity and mor-

tality outcomes (Supplemental Table 3).

## DISCUSSION

In this prespecified analysis of DAPA ACT HF-TIMI

68, we evaluated the effect of in-hospital initiation

of dapagliflozin on decongestion-related parameters

during the early postdischarge period among patients

hospitalized for HF. Several key findings emerged.

First, greater baseline congestion was independently

associated with higher risks of HF-related events and

death through 2 months. Second, dapagliflozin led to

modest but significant improvements across multiple

complementary measures of congestion, with treat-

ment effects evident by 1 week after randomization

and sustained through 2 months. Third, diuretic ef-

ficiency progressively improved over time with

dapagliflozin, reflecting sustained weight loss and

reduced background loop diuretic requirements.

Collectively, these findings demonstrate that

in-hospital initiation of dapagliflozin during HF

EFFECTS OF DAPAGLIFLOZIN ON DECONGESTION-

RELATED ENDPOINTS. Dapagliflozin favorably

affected multiple complementary measures of

congestion within 1 week of treatment initiation.

This temporal pattern is consistent with the known

natriuretic and osmotic diuretic effects of SGLT2 in-

hibitors. Interestingly, diuretic efficiency, a widely

recognized marker of decongestive efficacy,

continued to improve over time, driven by reduced

loop diuretic requirements. If these benefits were

mediated exclusively through early natriuresis and

osmotic diuresis, one would not expect these curves

to continue to diverge, particularly because the early

diuretic response is known to be rapidly offset by

increased water reabsorption in the more distal

segments of the nephron. 20 Instead, the pattern

observed in our study suggests that the sustained

favorable effects of dapagliflozin on congestion pa-

rameters may be related to effects beyond direct

diuretic augmentation.

Several mechanisms may contribute to this

observation. Experimental and clinical studies sug-

gest that SGLT2 inhibitors promote preferential

mobilization of interstitial fluid while preserving

intravascular volume, a profile that differs from

conventional loop diuretics. 21,22 SGLT2 inhibitors

have also been shown to restore tubuloglomerular

feedback, improve ventricular geometry and reduce

cardiac filling pressures, and modulate neurohor-

monal pathways that contribute to sodium and water

retention. 23,24 Whether these sustained improve-

ments reflect improved responsiveness to conven-

tional diuretic therapy or other disease-modifying

RELATIONSHIP TO CLINICAL OUTCOMES. Although

dapagliflozin did not significantly reduce the primary

composite endpoint of CVD or WHF through 60 days

in DAPA ACT HF-TIMI 68, the totality of randomized

trial data based on a meta-analysis of SOLOIST-WHF

(Effect of Sotagliflozin on Cardiovascular Events in

Patients with Type 2 Diabetes Post Worsening

Heart Failure), EMPULSE, and DAPA ACT HF-TIMI 68,

suggests that in-hospital initiation of SGLT2 in-

hibitors reduces the high risk of clinical events,

including all-cause mortality, in the early post-

discharge period. 8 Importantly, there was no evi-

dence that baseline congestion severity modified the

treatment effect of dapagliflozin on clinical out-

comes. These findings suggest that although

congestion identifies risk, it does not identify pa-

tients who preferentially benefit from SGLT2 in-

hibitors. Accordingly, congestion severity should not

be used to guide decisions regarding initiation of

SGLT2 inhibitors among otherwise eligible hospital-

ized patients.

CLINICAL IMPLICATIONS. HF hospitalization repre-

sents a critical opportunity to initiate evidence-

based HF therapies. Our findings demonstrate that

initiation of dapagliflozin after clinical stabilization

leads to early improvements across complementary

measures of congestion that persist through the

vulnerable postdischarge period. Together with the

established safety profile of in-hospital initiation of

SGLT2 inhibitors, these findings provide additional

support for implementation of SGLT2 inhibitors

during HF hospitalization rather than deferring

treatment until after discharge.

STUDY LIMITATIONS. First, congestion was assessed

using a CCS that relies on clinical assessment of signs

and symptoms. Although sites were prospectively

trained on the assessment of HF signs and symptoms,

and data were recorded on dedicated pages in the

electronic case report form (eCRF), the scoring sys-

tem can be subjective. Moreover, because the specific

study staff members performing the assessments

were not recorded in the eCRF and replicate assess-

ments by multiple observers were not required, we

are not able to formally assess interobserver reli-

ability. Second, some patients had missing conges-

tion data; however, multiple imputation methods

yielded treatment effects that were directionally

consistent with the primary analysis. Third, change

in body weight is an imperfect surrogate for fluid loss

in patients treated with SGLT2 inhibitors, because

SGLT2 inhibitors produce a net calorie deficit by

increasing glycosuria. However, the concurrent

reduction in loop diuretic dosing with dapagliflozin

supports the interpretation that the observed weight

loss is related to a decongestive effect. Fourth,

additional measures of decongestion, including bio-

markers, urine output, and invasive hemodynamics,

were not available and may have provided additional

mechanistic insight. Fifth, there was no adjustment

made for multiple comparisons; thus, the possibility

of chance findings among the multiple decongestion-

related endpoints and time points cannot be

excluded. Finally, follow-up was limited to 2 months,

precluding assessment of longer-term relationships

between changes in congestion parameters and clin-

ical outcomes. However, this study period encom-

passes the time period during which the

decongestive effects of SGLT2 inhibitors would be

expected to emerge and therefore is particularly

relevant to the objectives of this analysis.

## CONCLUSIONS

Among patients hospitalized for HF in DAPA ACT

HF-TIMI 68, greater baseline congestion identified

patients at higher risk of HF-related events and

death, reinforcing the potential value of therapies

that promote decongestion during hospitalization

and in the early postdischarge period. In-hospital

initiation of dapagliflozin led to improvements in

multiple clinically relevant measures of congestion

within 1 week of treatment initiation, with progres-

sive improvements in diuretic efficiency through

2 months. Although the temporal pattern of these

effects may not be attributable solely to direct

diuretic actions, the mechanisms underlying the

sustained decongestive effects cannot be determined

from this analysis. These findings provide further

insight into the role of SGLT2 inhibitors in patients

hospitalized for HF and support in-hospital initiation

of dapagliflozin following clinical stabilization.

## Abstract

The relationship between cystatin C and cardiovascular and kidney outcomes is not well explored in individuals with type 2 diabetes (T2D) and normal or mild kidney dysfunction.

This nested prospective biomarker study included patients enrolled in DECLARE-TIMI 58. Participants were categorized into quartiles of CysC/creatinine and eGFRCysC/eGFRCr and classified according to Kidney Disease Improving Global Outcomes (KDIGO) risk categories. Hazard ratios were estimated for a composite of cardiovascular death and hospitalization for heart failure (CVD/HHF), major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE), and a kidney-specific composite outcome (persistent ≥40% decrease in eGFR, end-stage renal disease, or renal death).

Among 1899 placebo-treated patients, higher baseline CysC was associated with higher risk for CVD/HHF, MACE, and the kidney-specific composite outcome. A gradient of risk across quartiles was observed for CVD/HHF [Q4 v Q1: 1.33 (0.98–1.80), p-trend = 0.016]; MACE [1.34 (1.06–1.69), p-trend = 0.013]; and kidney-specific composite outcome [1.95 (0.95–3.99), p-trend = 0.036]. When compared with creatinine, CysC showed more pronounced and statistically significant risk gradients (CVD/HHF: KDIGO-CysC p-trend < 0.001 vs. p-trend Cr 0.34; MACE: CysC p-trend < 0.001 vs. Cr p-trend 0.52). No heterogeneity was observed in the effect of dapagliflozin across CysC concentrations (p-interactions >0.05).

In patients with T2D and predominantly preserved Cr-based eGFR, CysC was associated with increased cardiovascular and kidney risk. Although discrimination assessed by c-statistic was similar for CysC and Cr, risk gradients seen with CysC became attenuated and no longer statistically significant when using Cr-based analogs. The effect of dapagliflozin was consistent irrespective of baseline CysC.

## Introduction

Cystatin C (CysC), a low-molecular-weight protein secreted by all human nucleated cells at a constant rate, is freely filtered by the renal glomerulus and metabolized by proximal tubular cells [1]. CysC has been suggested as an alternative to serum creatinine (Cr) for estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) because its production is less influenced by non-GFR factors, including age, sex, muscle mass, physical activity, nutritional status, and protein intake [2], [3], [4], [5]. Prior studies have suggested that in addition to more precisely calculating eGFR, circulating CysC levels are independently associated with cardiovascular risk [6], [7], [8]. While CysC has been shown to be an accurate and reliable marker of kidney function and a predictive biomarker for cardiovascular and kidney risk, there remains a need to understand its utility across various patient populations.

Diabetes is a leading cause of chronic kidney disease (CKD), a significant risk factor for cardiovascular morbidity and death [9]. The ability of CysC, compared to Cr, to predict risk of cardiovascular and kidney outcomes in patients with type 2 diabetes (T2D) and predominantly preserved kidney function is less certain. Examining the predictive role of CysC in a cohort of T2D patients with predominantly preserved Cr-based eGFR may inform the use of CysC-based alternatives to Cr-based measures in clinical scenarios where Cr measurements may be less reliable. Albuminuria, a component of diabetic kidney disease, is associated with an increased risk for all-cause and cardiovascular mortality in patients with diabetes [10]. Improved cardiovascular risk prediction has been demonstrated in patients with CKD through the use of Cr-based eGFR and albuminuria utilizing risk categories established by the Kidney Disease Improving Global Outcomes (KDIGO) guidelines incorporating both measures [11], [12]. Less is known about the predictive ability of the combined assessment of CysC-based estimated GFR (eGFRCysC) and albuminuria for both cardiovascular and kidney outcomes.

Dapagliflozin is a sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 inhibitor (SGLT2i), a class of medications that lower blood sugar and have consistently shown favorable cardiovascular and kidney effects in patients with and without T2D [13]. The Dapagliflozin Effect on Cardiovascular Events (DECLARE)–TIMI 58 trial evaluated dapagliflozin vs. placebo among patients with T2D and either multiple risk factors for atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease or established cardiovascular disease [14]. This trial demonstrated a significant 17% reduction in cardiovascular death or hospitalization for heart failure with dapagliflozin and a reduction in the progression of kidney disease [15]. In the current study, we assessed the association between CysC and Cr and risk of cardiovascular and kidney outcomes in a population with T2D and predominantly preserved Cr-based eGFR. In addition, we investigated the treatment effect of dapagliflozin compared to placebo according to baseline CysC concentrations.

## Methods

### Study population

This was a nested biomarker substudy from DECLARE-TIMI 58. The trial design, baseline characteristics, and main results have previously been published [14], [15], [16]. In brief, DECLARE-TIMI 58 was a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled, multinational trial of dapagliflozin among 17,160 patients with T2D and either established atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease (ASCVD) [age ≥40 years and either ischemic heart disease, cerebrovascular disease, or peripheral arterial disease] or multiple risk factors for ASCVD (age ≥55 years for men or ≥60 years for women plus at least one of dyslipidemia, hypertension, or current tobacco use) and a creatinine clearance (CrCl) of ≥60 mL/min. Eligibility for DECLARE-TIMI 58 required CrCl ≥60 mL/min at screening, estimated using the Cockcroft-Gault equation. Because kidney function was reassessed at randomization using CKD-EPI eGFR, some participants had baseline eGFR <60 mL/min/1.73 m2 despite meeting the screening eligibility criterion [17]. The trial protocol, including the biomarker substudy, was approved by the institutional review board at each participating site and all participants provided written informed consent.

### Outcomes of interest

The trial had dual primary efficacy endpoints: a composite of cardiovascular death (CVD) and hospitalization for heart failure (HHF) and major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE, a composite of CVD, myocardial infarction, or ischemic stroke). A kidney-specific composite outcome (persistent ≥40% decrease in eGFR, end-stage renal disease, or renal death) was also evaluated [14], [15]. All components of the primary outcomes were adjudicated in a blinded manner by an independent clinical events committee using previously published definitions [14]. The change in eGFR for the kidney composite outcome was calculated based on creatinine measured in a central laboratory.

### Study design

We designed a nested prospective biomarker study among patients enrolled in the biomarker substudy of DECLARE-TIMI 58. The analysis of the association between CysC and cardiovascular and kidney outcomes included 1899 placebo-treated subjects. The full cohort of 3698 patients in whom CysC was measured was used for the analysis of any effect modification with dapagliflozin. We utilized a case-cohort design. Cases were determined by the presence of the respective outcomes of interest, and controls were selected from a random sample of the entire cohort with no restrictions. Hazard ratios were determined according to baseline CysC and CysC-based measures of kidney function with multivariable adjustment.

### Biomarkers

Blood samples were collected on the day of randomization and isolated plasma was stored at -20°C or colder until shipped on dry ice to the TIMI Clinical Trials Laboratory (Boston, Massachusetts). Serum cystatin C (CysC) was measured using a commercially available immunoturbidimetric assay (Roche Diagnostics, Indianapolis, IN).

### Measures of kidney function

The Cr-based eGFR was determined by using the 2012 Chronic Kidney Disease Epidemiology Collaboration (CKD-EPI) Creatinine Equation [18]. CysC-based eGFR was calculated using the 2012 CKD-EPI Cystatin C Equation [19].

We categorized participants by quartiles of baseline CysC/Cr and eGFRCysC/eGFRCr. In addition, we classified participants according to KDIGO risk categories defined by eGFRCysC/eGFRCr and albuminuria at baseline [20]. When classified by eGFR alone, categories were condensed as ≥90, 60 to <90, and <60 mL/min/1.73 m2. For KDIGO risk classification, participants were categorized into the established KDIGO risk groups (low, moderate, high, and very high risk) using the KDIGO combined eGFR and albuminuria categories. Albuminuria was categorized as A1 (normal to mildly increased; ACR <30 mg/g), A2 (moderately increased; ACR 30–300 mg/g), or A3 (severely increased; ACR >300 mg/g).

### Statistical analyses

Baseline characteristics are presented according to quartiles of baseline CysC. Continuous variables are summarized as medians (interquartile ranges [IQRs]) and categorical variables as counts and percentages. The p-trend for each outcome represents a test of trend across quartiles using the Cochran Armitage trend test for categorical covariates and the Jonckheere-Terpstra test for continuous covariates. The associations between biomarker measures and outcomes were examined within the placebo arm using Cox proportional hazard regression models adjusted for age, sex, race, smoking, history of heart failure, body mass index, T2D duration, insulin use, baseline albuminuria, coronary artery disease, myocardial infarction, ischemic stroke, peripheral artery disease, dyslipidemia, and hypertension. P-values for trend across quartiles were derived from the corresponding adjusted Cox proportional hazards models using the same covariates. Harrell's C-statistic with corresponding 95% confidence intervals was used to assess model discrimination [21]. In sensitivity analyses, Cr-based eGFR and corresponding KDIGO risk categories were recalculated using the 2021 CKD-EPI creatinine equation. As an exploratory analysis, category-free net reclassification improvement (NRI) was calculated to assess whether addition of CysC improved risk classification beyond a model incorporating creatinine-based eGFR. To explore the non-linear association between biomarker concentrations and the treatment effect of dapagliflozin for each outcome in the full cohort of 3698 patients, we further fit Cox models with CysC concentrations using restricted cubic splines. Two-sided p-values <0.05 were considered to indicate nominal statistical significance. SAS v9.4 (SAS Institute, Cary, NC) was used for the analysis.

## Results

### Study population

Among the 3698 participants in the full cohort, 2429 patients were male, the median age was 64.0 (60.0, 69.0), and the median (25th, 75th percentile) duration of type 2 diabetes was 11.0 (6.0, 17.0) years (Table 1). No significant difference was found in baseline characteristics between the 1899 placebo-treated subjects included in the primary analysis population and the full cohort of 3698 patients with a CysC measurement (Supplemental Table S1). At baseline, 192 of 1899 participants (10.1%) in the placebo-treated primary analysis cohort had a Cr-based eGFR <60 mL/min/1.73 m2. CysC levels ranged from 0.2 to 3.7 mg/L with a median of 0.93 mg/L. Subjects with higher baseline CysC levels tended to be older and were more likely to have a history of heart failure, peripheral artery disease, coronary artery disease, and cerebrovascular disease. HbA1c levels were similar across quartiles. Baseline UACR was available in 3644 of 3698 participants, with a median UACR of 15.5 mg/g (IQR 6.5–53.4); 66% had UACR <30 mg/g.

### Relationship between cystatin C and cardiovascular and kidney outcomes

Among those allocated to placebo, patients with higher baseline CysC levels had higher rates of CVD/HHF, MACE, and the kidney-specific composite outcome after multivariable adjustment (Fig. 1). Application of CysC-based KDIGO risk categories, which also incorporate albuminuria, identified a very high-risk group (n = 167) (Fig. 1). C-statistics were not significantly different across the measures.

### Comparing cystatin C and creatinine measures

Though overall discrimination assessed by c-statistic was similar with CysC compared to Cr across biomarker quartiles, eGFR, and KDIGO risk categories, the risk gradients with Cr-based measures were generally attenuated and did not meet statistical significance (Fig. 1). Sensitivity analyses using the 2021 CKD-EPI creatinine equation resulted in limited reclassification and did not materially alter the overall associations observed with Cr-based eGFR quartiles or KDIGO risk categories (Supplemental Table S2).

### Treatment effect of dapagliflozin according to baseline cystatin C levels

The treatment effect of dapagliflozin was consistent irrespective of baseline CysC levels for CVD/HHF, MACE, and kidney-specific composite outcome. There was no evidence for heterogeneity in the effect of dapagliflozin across the continuous biomarker concentration (p-interaction >0.05) for all measured outcomes (Fig. 2).

### Risk reclassification with cystatin C

In exploratory analyses, addition of CysC to a model incorporating Cr-based eGFR resulted in category-free NRIs of 0.11 (95% CI, 0.02 to 0.20) for MACE, 0.07 (−0.04 to 0.18) for CVD/HHF, and 0.19 (−0.03 to 0.40) for the kidney-specific composite outcome (Supplemental Table S3). Results were directionally consistent in sensitivity analyses using the 2021 CKD-EPI equation.

## Discussion

In this analysis from the DECLARE-TIMI 58 trial, among patients with T2D who were eligible based on initially preserved kidney function, higher CysC concentrations were associated with increased risk for CVD/HHF, MACE, and the kidney-specific composite outcome after multivariable adjustment. Overall discrimination assessed by c-statistic was similar with CysC compared with Cr across biomarker quartiles, eGFR, and KDIGO risk categories. However, the significant risk gradients seen with the CysC-based measurements generally became attenuated when using Cr-based analogs and no longer met statistical significance. We found no evidence of heterogeneity in the effect of dapagliflozin across CysC concentration for any of these endpoints. Nevertheless, CysC may identify higher-risk patients who warrant closer monitoring and optimization of cardiovascular and kidney risk-reduction strategies because of their potential for greater absolute benefits with established therapies.

Traditionally, eGFRCr has been the standard for clinical assessment of kidney function and is used in the classification of patients with CKD [22]. Limitations inherent to creatinine as a biomarker, particularly variability introduced by non-GFR determinants, can obscure underlying risk signals [19], [23], [24]. CysC-based measures demonstrated independent risk gradients for cardiovascular and kidney outcomes after adjustment for multiple covariates. GFR estimation is an especially important clinical tool to screen for CKD in high-risk groups, such as those with T2D. Despite these findings, CysC is not currently widely used in clinical practice to assess kidney function in part due to having not been validated in different patient groups with varying levels of kidney function and due to limitations in cost-effectiveness [25]. Distinct non-GFR determinants of CysC have been documented, including use of steroids, thyroid dysfunction, adiposity, and inflammation [26]. Compared to Cr, CysC appears to be affected by fewer factors, exhibits a lesser degree of susceptibility, and is more uniformly produced across diverse populations [1].

Taken together with our findings, the advantages of CysC, particularly its susceptibility to fewer non-GFR determinants, support a role for CysC alongside creatinine in risk assessment for patients with T2D and preserved baseline Cr-based eGFR. Moreover, the numerically greater risk gradient observed with the combined assessment of eGFRCysC and albuminuria suggests enhanced risk stratification compared to CysC or eGFRCysC alone. Our findings highlight the clinical relevance of CysC as a complementary biomarker to creatinine to enhance risk stratification among patients with T2D who have predominantly preserved baseline Cr-based eGFR.

### Limitations

Our findings reflect the baseline characteristics of this clinical trial study population. This population has a narrower range of kidney function than the general T2D population due to the enrollment criteria. However, it is possible that these relationships could be stronger when studied in a population with a broader range of kidney function and may help to identify a population with worse CysC-based kidney function that has greater benefit from SGLT2i. DECLARE-TIMI 58 eligibility required CrCl ≥60 mL/min at screening. Kidney function was subsequently reassessed at the randomization visit using CKD-EPI eGFR. Therefore, some participants had eGFR <60 mL/min/1.73 m2 at randomization despite meeting the screening eligibility criterion. Classification of kidney function based on a single measurement is a limitation of this analysis. Although enrollment required preserved Cr-based eGFR at screening, albuminuria was not an enrollment criterion, and approximately one-third of participants had baseline UACR ≥30 mg/g. We had no direct measures of muscle mass or clinical conditions that may influence CysC levels, though our data included surrogates for these characteristics, including age and BMI. We therefore cannot specifically comment on these relationships. Racial and ethnic minority groups were underrepresented in the trial population compared with the general population with T2D, limiting our ability to assess the potential added utility of CysC in these populations.

## Conclusions

In this population with T2D and predominantly preserved Cr-based eGFR, CysC-based measures of kidney function were independently associated with CVD/HHF, MACE, and a kidney-specific composite outcome with significant risk gradients across quartiles, eGFR, and KDIGO risk categories. Dapagliflozin had a consistent effect across the entire spectrum of CysC with respect to CVD/HHF, MACE, and kidney-specific composite outcome.

# Advancing Health Equity in the Cardiovascular Device Life Cycle

**Authors:** Andre M. Small; Nathan W. Watson; Rishi K. Wadhera; Eric A. Secemsky; Robert W. Yeh

**Affiliations:** 1Department of Medicine, Brigham and Women’s Hospital, Harvard Medical School, Boston, MA | 2Smith Center for Outcomes Research in Cardiology, Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center, Harvard Medical School, Boston, MA | 3Division of Cardiology, Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center, Harvard Medical School, Boston, MA

## Abstract

Despite advancements in diagnostics and therapeutics for cardiovascular (CV) disease, significant health disparities persist among patients from historically marginalized racial and ethnic groups, women, individuals who are socioeconomically under-resourced or underinsured, and those living in rural communities. While transcatheter interventions have revolutionized the treatment landscape in cardiology, populations bearing the greatest burden of disease continue to face inequitable access and poorer outcomes. A notable gap in the literature concerns the role of modern approaches to CV device innovation in shaping and perpetuating health disparities. Health equity has been declared one of the top strategic initiatives for 2022–2025 by the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) Center for Devices and Radiological Health (CDRH), underscoring the need for greater attention, dialogue, and targeted interventions in this space. This narrative review uses the CV device life cycle as a conceptual framework to enhance understanding and guide future efforts to mitigate disparities in the field of interventional cardiology. Drawing on illustrative examples from interventional cardiology, we examine current practices in CV device regulation and approval, clinical trial evaluation, adoption patterns, and post-procedural outcomes with the aim of uncovering potential mechanisms of disparities and identifying opportunities for targeted interventions.

## Introduction

Cardiovascular (CV) disease remains the leading cause of death worldwide, estimated to affect more than 500 million individuals globally (1,2). Novel CV interventions have emerged over the past several decades (3,4). Despite these advancements, significant disparities in access, treatment, and outcomes for CV disease persist (5–7).

CV devices may be particularly prone to the generation and propagation of health disparities, as they are often characterized by resource-intensive delivery, availability primarily concentrated in tertiary referral centers, requirements for highly specialized operator expertise, lack of universal reimbursement by insurers, and phased rollouts governed by industry incentives. Data have shown that populations at high risk for CV disease, including patients from historically marginalized racial and ethnic groups, women, individuals who are socioeconomically under-resourced or underinsured, and those living in rural communities have disproportionately limited access to novel CV devices despite bearing the greatest burden of CV disease (8,9).

This intersection between medical device epidemiology and health equity has been broadly recognized as being an important public health challenge by numerous stakeholders including patients, physicians, device manufacturers, regulators, and policymakers. To this point, health equity has been declared as one of the top strategic initiatives for 2022–2025 by the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) Center for Devices and Radiological Health (CDRH), the organization that governs medical device evaluation and approval in the United States (10).

In this narrative review, we draw upon illustrative examples in the field of interventional cardiology to examine current practices in CV device regulation and approval, clinical trial evaluation, adoption patterns, and post-procedural outcomes (Figure 1). We aim to elucidate potential mechanisms of disparities and identify opportunities for targeted interventions at each step in the CV device life cycle.

### Equity Implications of Regulatory Approval Frameworks Remain Underexplored

Examination of the regulatory and approval frameworks for novel CV devices may highlight upstream factors contributing to disparities and assist in guiding targeted policy interventions. The 1976 Medical Device Amendments to the Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act of 1938 expanded the FDA’s authority to oversee the premarket approval and risk classification of medical devices and currently serves as the primary regulatory framework for new devices in the United States (11). Subsequent legislative efforts over the last four decades have targeted medical device regulatory pathways to limit unnecessary requirements, expand access to novel devices, and fulfill specific public health needs. Specifically, the FDA Modernization Act of 1997 directed the FDA to reduce the premarket data requirements by relying on post-market surveillance to expand access to investigational devices (12). The implications of streamlining device regulatory systems on patient safety, particularly among populations at higher risk for CV disease, remains underexplored. CV devices face a notable challenge because, despite their life-saving potential, they frequently account for the highest proportion of reported adverse events among high-risk devices and are linked to the largest share of the FDA’s most critical recalls (13). The understanding of how these policies affect the safety, utilization rates, and outcomes among patients at the highest risk for CV disease is limited.

In 2016, Congress authorized the FDA Breakthrough Devices Program (BDP) to stimulate medical device innovation and expedite patient access to novel devices deemed breakthrough technologies (14). As expected, shorter regulatory review times for CV devices have been associated with a higher relative frequency of adverse event reports (13). Moreover, it has previously been hypothesized that the BDP may have additional adverse effects on health equity due to underrepresentation in premarketing studies as well as challenges with accessibility and affordability for some populations (15). Large international studies have demonstrated that longer FDA regulatory approval processes for CV devices may lead to meaningful patient safety benefits (16). This highlights the policy conundrum of striking a balance between ensuring timely access to novel CV devices and conducting thorough premarket evaluation. While this tension is well-recognized in a broad context, the differential effects of such policies on patient populations with higher baseline CV risk remains underexplored.

Consider an example of how evolving evidentiary standards for regulatory approval of medical devices may inadvertently compromise health equity. Studies have demonstrated that increased utilization of expedited regulatory pathways often rely more heavily on surrogate measures, some of which have unclear clinical significance (17). This reliance on surrogate markers may contribute to misconceptions regarding the effectiveness and necessity of certain CV interventions, particularly in linguistically and culturally diverse patient populations. The invasive and high-risk nature of CV procedures, coupled with historical injustices that have fueled growing mistrust among historically marginalized groups towards the healthcare industry, highlights the unique potential for CV interventions to fuel disparities in CV disease (18). Furthermore, devices authorized through the BDP are more likely to be rolled out in prominent tertiary care facilities, potentially restricting access to populations reliant on under-resourced medical facilities and lacking adequate insurance coverage. Further studies are needed on the extent to which contractual processes between healthcare systems and device manufacturers (e.g., pre-approval purchasing agreements with hospitals) enable inequitable dissemination of novel devices.

In 2014, Rome et al delineated important implications of the regulatory approval processes for high-risk medical devices within clinical cardiology (19). Among the implications highlighted were the variable evidentiary standards for studying investigational devices for safety and effectiveness, the increasing dependence on post-approval studies despite the limited authority of the FDA to mandate such studies, and the legal ramifications ensuing from device approval pathway. While their original analysis focused on general implications, examination through a health equity lens can shed light on how these limitations disproportionately affect populations at higher risk. Limited FDA authority to mandate post-approval studies and weak legal protections for patients are likely to inflict more harm to patients without the resources and advocacy to navigate complex legal pathways. Strengthening the FDA’s involvement in rigorous post-market surveillance to monitor CV device performance and safety outcomes, with incentives for detecting disparities in outcomes, may provide valuable insights into whether specific groups experience greater benefits or harm. Legislative reforms to strengthen legal protections for patients harmed by FDA-approved devices can further promote equity.

An executive summary, published by the FDA in September 2023, highlighted the outcomes of an advisory committee meeting focused on advancing health equity in medical devices (20). This summary outlines significant challenges associated with proposed regulatory principles, particularly in ensuring inclusivity, data generalizability, and timely access to innovative medical devices. One key challenge outlined in this document explains that providing timely access to innovative devices goes beyond market authorization. For example, a cross-sectional analysis of 64 medical devices authorized by the FDA between 2016–2019 revealed that, among the 44% of these devices which required establishing new Medicare coverage, it took a median of 5.7 years to obtain coverage (21). These extended timelines in establishing Medicare coverage present a policy opportunity to ensure more extensive coverage for novel devices, particularly those expected to have a large impact on the care of populations at higher risk for CV disease.

A recently published American Heart Association (AHA) Scientific Statement in 2024 on the use of artificial intelligence (AI) in improving outcomes in heart disease noted that “a new understanding of inclusion will involve forms of context-aware technical development, and innovative, local- and community-led approaches aiming the redesign, deployment, and validation of digital technologies (22).” The statement highlights a need for AI and machine learning models to combat data bias, noting that the perspectives among populations most harmed by algorithmic bias are underrepresented in algorithm development. Akin to the AHA’s stance on AI, we contend that there is a critical need to reassess our regulatory frameworks for novel CV devices through this discerning perspective with active involvement of historically marginalized and underserved patient populations. Further strategies may include patient consultants on device development teams to ensure the development of novel CV devices are meeting the needs of higher risk populations, as well as employing health equity experts in clinical trial leadership to ensure future studies intentionally prioritize health equity.

### Device Trials Lack Representative Populations

Research has highlighted ongoing challenges in recruiting diverse populations for CV device clinical trials (23). To address these concerns, the 2014 FDA Action Plan attempted to diversify clinical trial enrollment, emphasizing the completeness of demographic data, identification of barriers to enrollment within sub-populations, and increasing transparency in demographic data (24). In the following year, among 42 original premarket devices, a substantial proportion of studies utilized for FDA approval incompletely reported demographic data, including age, race and ethnicity, and sex (25). Furthermore, in device labels, age was reported in only 7% of studies, while race and ethnicity were reported in just 1%, and sex in 16% (25). Safety and efficacy data for high-risk devices are often still difficult to determine due to the lack of publicly available data (26). Limited data on the safety and effectiveness of investigational CV devices across diverse patient populations limit our ability to extrapolate clinical outcomes to groups who are at disproportionately higher risk for disease.

Guidance documents from the FDA have offered practical strategies to improve diversity in clinical trials, emphasizing the selection of trial sites with diverse populations, multilingual approaches to information distribution, flexibility in enrollment criteria, reducing participation burdens, community outreach, and digital health technologies (27–29). These recommendations highlight the importance of collecting standardized race and ethnicity data for prespecified subgroup analyses to better understand device safety and effectiveness in diverse populations. Landmark legislation recently signed by President Biden in the Consolidated Appropriations Act of 2023 is a more recent effort to address the issue of clinical trial diversity (30). The Act mandates that investigational studies of drugs and devices include a diversity action plan that comprehensively considers participant demographics and specific enrollment goals that consider three key factors: the estimated prevalence or incidence of the disease or condition being studied, the characteristics of the intended patient population, and the potential obstacles to enrolling a diverse range of patients in clinical trials.

Recent data suggest that little progress has been made despite calls for diversity and representation in CV research studies. In a comprehensive study involving 153 landmark CV randomized clinical trials conducted over the past decade, nearly half of the trials did not report racial or ethnicity data, and there has been no notable advancement in the inclusion of traditionally underrepresented racial and ethnic groups in these studies (31). The limited progress in inclusivity of underrepresented groups has been partly attributed to the increasing globalization of clinical trials outside the United States (32). Several strategies have been proposed to diversify trial participants including improving the diversity of clinical trial leadership, incorporating race and ethnicity data in the site selection process, and outreach efforts focused on recruitment from communities of color (33). A combination of federal incentives and regulations has been proposed (34). Such recommendations include increased federal funding directed at enhancing enrollment capacity at trial sites serving underrepresented populations, financial incentives to drug manufacturers based on representative trial enrollment (e.g., tax credit), and implementation of an FDA requirement that representative enrollment in post-approval studies begins before drug approval (34). Future efforts to enhance clinical trial diversity must also acknowledge the challenges that are unique to novel CV devices, such as variable approval pathways and the need for highly specialized provider expertise.

Previous work has outlined systematic frameworks aimed to enhance the enrollment of under-resourced patient populations in clinical trials, with a particular focus on heart failure therapeutics. These efforts highlighted the importance of engaging multiple stakeholders including patients, communities, research design and sponsorship, and regulatory bodies (35). We propose that a similarly comprehensive approach could more effectively address disparities in the broader CV device landscape.

### Barriers to Equitable Dissemination of Novel CV Devices

Following the completion of clinical trials and regulatory approval, novel CV devices are often introduced into clinical practice in ways that may deepen health inequities. These patterns stem from the complex referral system for advanced technologies and resource-intensive nature of interventional CV care, as well as issues related to the geographic distribution of novel CV devices.

#### Complex Referral and Treatment Pathways Limit Access and Delivery

The decision to pursue an invasive CV intervention involves a complex series of steps beginning with the onset of symptoms to referral for subspecialty management and procedural care (36). Each step along this treatment pathway is susceptible to inequities (37). Potential barriers include inadequate access to primary and specialty care services, costly screening and diagnostic testing, lower rates of referral to proceduralists, disparities inherent within procedural planning, and differences in post-procedural monitoring and outcomes (38–41). Differential treatment decisions may arise at each stage, influenced by factors such as interpersonal bias, limited cultural competency efforts, and individual patient health preferences or mistrust in the healthcare system (42–45).

The complex referral process as a mechanism of inequitable dissemination of CV devices was studied in the late 1990s and early 2000s with the emerging prevalence of cardiac catheterization and percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) (46). By the late 1990s, it was well-established that Black Americans underwent interventional therapy for coronary artery disease at rates far lower than White Americans (47,48). However, the reasons for this disparity were not precisely known, and numerous studies attempted to better elucidate this mechanism. One such study conducted by Schulman and colleagues (1999) sought to evaluate CV provider’s decisions to refer patients for diagnostic cardiac catheterization for the evaluation of chest pain (49). In this study, physicians were shown scripted interviews of patients of varying races and sexes and instructed to provide management decisions. Investigators found that Black race and specifically Black women were significantly less likely to be referred for cardiac catheterization as compared to White patients (49). Similar findings were found in a more contemporary study of physicians allocating therapies for advanced heart failure. In this work, physicians were randomized to clinical vignettes which differed regarding the patient’s race. Dramatic gender and racial bias were found in the decision-making process for utilizing advanced heart failure therapeutics such heart transplantation or ventricular assist devices (VAD) (50). These findings were also particularly evident among Black women, who were found to be judged more harshly for their appearance and social support systems (51). Moreover, these findings have been replicated in another study that also found that allocation of transplant and VADs was lower among Black patients even after adjustment for disease severity and other social determinants of health (52). Updated data regarding racial and gender bias in the decision-making process for heart transplant candidacy was recently reported. In a study leveraging data between October 2018 and March 2023, the cumulative incidence of heart offer acceptance by a transplant center team was consistently lower for Black candidates than for White candidates of the same gender after adjusting for candidate-, donor-, and offer-level variables (53). Additionally, similar findings have been evident among patients of lower SES. In one study investigating nearly 17,000 patients presenting with an acute myocardial infarction (MI), primary PCI was utilized less frequently among the lowest income cohort (54). However, more recent work has suggested lower income groups receive similar care for ST-elevation MI, possibly due to the expansion of PCI centers across the US over the last decade (55).

Access to state-of-the-art devices for peripheral artery disease (PAD) have also faced significant racial disparities, particularly in Black communities (56). Multiple studies conducted over the past two decades have consistently shown that Black patients are less likely to undergo revascularization procedures for PAD, resulting in a higher likelihood of major amputations (57). In one study among patients with chronic limb threatening ischemia (CLTI), Black patients were nearly twofold more likely to receive an amputation as compared to White patients. These disparities in amputation rates were most apparent in areas with the greatest access to resources, such as increasing hospital revascularization capacity (58,59). Moreover, other studies have also found differential amputation rates among certain geographic regions, particular within the Southern US (60). Similar findings were also demonstrated in a study among Medicare beneficiaries who underwent lower extremity major amputation. Among this sample of amputees, Black patients were significantly less likely to have received a revascularization procedure within the prior two years as compared to White patients (61).

Potential drivers of these disparities can be linked to the unique treatment and referral process of CV devices. Limited access to primary and subspecialty care, bias in the referral and decision-making process for advanced therapies, inequities in insurance coverage and cost-sharing which disproportionately impacts patients from lower SES backgrounds, and incentives for providers to take on patients with insurance coverage offering high reimbursement (e.g., commercial vs Medicaid) may underlie these disparities. Efforts aimed at streamlining the referral process and addressing barriers inherent to under-resourced populations, including educational campaigns and subsidies to offset financial barriers may result in a more equitable approach to delivering CV devices to all patients.

#### Inequitable Adoption Patterns Reinforce Disparities

A growing body of research has demonstrated inequitable geographic dissemination of novel CV technologies. One contemporary example within the field of interventional cardiology is the Transcatheter Aortic Valve Replacement (TAVR) procedure for severe aortic stenosis. Racial, ethnic, socioeconomic, and geographic characteristics have been associated with access, dissemination, utilization, and outcomes related to TAVR procedure (8,9,62–64). In an evaluation of Medicare beneficiaries who underwent TAVR between 2012 and 2018, the establishment of TAVR programs was predominately located within areas with a lower proportion of patients with dual eligibility for Medicaid and an overall higher median household income with concentrated growth in regions with existing TAVR programs (8). While these findings may be supported when considered on a per capita basis, it is possible that lower reimbursements for hospitals serving economically under-resourced communities may affect procedural availability. To further investigate this possibility, a multicenter, nationwide cross-sectional analysis of Medicare claims data was conducted to better understand the association between zip code-level racial, ethnic, and socioeconomic composition and the receipt of TAVR (8). The study found that rates of TAVR utilization were lower in zip codes with a higher proportions of Black and Hispanic patients despite adjusting for socioeconomic markers, age, and other clinical comorbidities (8). These findings persisted irrespective of geographic proximity to hospital sites offering the procedure and their level of health insurance coverage (8). Another important consideration is the potential influence of insurance status on a patient’s likelihood of receiving a CV intervention. This notion is substantiated by prior research, which revealed that patients with Medicaid or no health insurance were significantly less likely to receive a drug-eluting stent compared to those with private insurance (65). Inequitable adoption patterns have also been described in endovascular therapy (EVT) for ischemic stroke, with Black patients being less likely to receive EVT compared to White patients despite similar rates of admission to EVT-performing hospitals (66). Moreover, similar findings were found among the selection of patients for catheter ablation for atrial fibrillation (67). These findings have relevance for other established and emerging CV technologies.

Other work has suggested that growth of novel CV technologies may not be proportional to the overall disease burden or growth of the population. This phenomenon was highlighted in the 2000s with the expansion of PCI within the United States. Between 2003 and 2011, the number PCI centers grew by 21.2%, considerably outpacing population growth despite a declining prevalence of MI. This consequently resulted in geographic imbalances relative to need in some regions (68). The implementation of PCI centers most frequently occurred in the proximity of areas with higher private insurance coverage as well as in larger, wealthier hospitals (37). Additionally, its introduction was less frequent in states with regulatory measures, such as Certificate of Need programs, to review the establishment of new PCI programs (37). Data analyzing 2,388,180 patients with acute MI from 2006–2017 has underscored disparities in the admission rates and provision of specialized cardiac care among historically marginalized racial and ethnic groups compared to White patients. To explore potential contributors, researchers investigated whether the geographic distribution of specialized cardiac services played a role, analyzing differential changes in patient outcomes following the establishment of PCI-capable facilities (PCI-CF) by patient race and residential segregation (segregated vs integrated, using a dissimilarity index) levels (69). They found that Black patients in integrated communities demonstrated the greatest benefit across all outcomes measured, including a 5 times greater likelihood of receiving same-day PCI after a PCI-CF opening compared with White patients in segregated communities. These data provide critical public health insights and potential opportunities for improving PCI resource allocation, such as providing financial incentives to promote PCI-CF openings in predominantly Black and integrated communities and structural reform addressing the healthcare service environment.

A study involving 9,303 US adults in 2019 and 2020 revealed patterns of use of wearable devices among individuals with or at risk for CV disease (70). Their findings demonstrated that older age and lower household income were associated with a reduced odds of utilizing a wearable device, with challenges such as cost and technological accessibility for older individuals cited as barriers. Although the utilization of a commercially available wearable device differs fundamentally from receiving advanced interventional care, these findings underscore the importance of equitable adoption strategies, particularly for novel CV devices that may mitigate health disparities. While studies may demonstrate favorable outcomes with novel CV devices, without equitable adoption strategies, these benefits will remain inaccessible to many patients. Future studies further expanding our knowledge of equitable adoption strategies are necessary to further under this mechanism of health inequities.

### Post-Procedural Outcomes Are Unequal

The role of numerous health inequities in driving differential outcomes following PCI for coronary artery disease and acute MI has been extensively defined (71–73). Variation in outcomes described across different populations have often inappropriately been attributed to the greater prevalence and severity of medical comorbidities and disease risk factors such as hypertension, obesity, and diabetes. In a large study pooling nearly 23,000 patients from 10 randomized controlled trials, investigators found that baseline comorbidities were significantly more likely to be present in racial and ethnic minority groups than White patients. However, even after controlling for these differences, Black race remained a positive predictor of worse clinical outcomes following PCI (74). Moreover, others have also found that Black and female patients are more likely to experience worse quality of life outcomes such as post-discharge angina following PCI for acute MI (75). In a study evaluating the association between race and neighborhood income on major adverse cardiac events (MACE) following PCI, investigators demonstrated that higher rates of MACE was associated with Black Americans and neighborhood incomes, driven largely by worse risk factor profiles at baseline (76).

Disparities in clinical outcomes following revascularization has also been described among patients with PAD undergoing peripheral endovascular intervention (56,77). Over the last decade, the landscape of interventional therapy for PAD has transformed and endovascular interventions are now the primary modality of revascularization (78). Nevertheless, recent studies have suggested that disparities in outcomes exist following endovascular therapy like what was observed with conventional surgical modalities. Krawisz and colleagues (2022) conducted a study among fee-for-service Medicare beneficiaries who underwent femoropopliteal endovascular intervention for PAD. This study found that Black patients were more likely to undergo peripheral interventions; however, these patients were also significantly more likely to present with advanced disease (i.e. CLTI) and experience adverse events such as death or major amputation than White patients. This group found that a high burden of comorbidities were largely responsible for these disparities among Black patients (77). Socioeconomic status also appears to play a role in differential outcomes following lower extremity revascularization. In a study among patients presenting for either open or endovascular revascularization, lower income status was associated with a more advanced clinical presentation, older patients, and lack of utilization of guideline-endorsed medical therapy prior to interventional management (79).

Furthermore, the link between health inequities and outcomes following device interventions has been described in patients undergoing TAVR for severe aortic stenosis (8,80). In a meta-analysis of three studies investigating TAVR, higher rates of adverse events such as post-procedure MI, acute kidney injury, and permanent pacemaker implantation were observed among Black patients compared to White patients (81). However, in an analysis of the American College of Cardiology/Society of Thoracic Surgeons/Transcatheter Valve Therapy Registry including over 70,000 patients receiving TAVR, after risk-adjustment, rates of both in-hospital and out-of-hospital complications were similar between all racial groups investigated (62). The root causes underlying worse risk profiles among Black patients have historically been mistakenly presumed to reflect biological or genetic differences across racial groups. A presidential advisory published by the American Heart Association (AHA) in 2020 outlined the impacts of structural racism, defined as “the normalization and legitimization of an array of dynamics—historical, cultural, institutional and interpersonal—that routinely advantage White people while producing cumulative and chronic adverse outcomes for people of color,” as a fundamental cause of persistent health disparities in the US (82). The effects of structural racism continue to persist with far-reaching consequences for CV health among Black patient populations across a variety of disciplines, including the justice system, education, access to capital, housing and living conditions, and access to health care. These factors have been linked to toxic stress and increased CV disease and stroke risk factors, which account for poorer health outcomes among Black patients. We contend with the recommendations outline by the AHA to effectively address health disparities, such as transforming conditions for historically marginalized communities through improved housing, neighborhoods, and equitable access to economic opportunities, education, and health care.

## Conclusion

In this narrative review, we examined disparities throughout the CV device life cycle, analyzing modern regulatory approval pathways, clinical trial design and recruitment, adoption patterns, and post-procedural outcomes. We proposed strategic directions aimed at advancing equity and improving outcomes for populations at the highest risk for CV disease with a focus on the field of interventional cardiology. While we are encouraged by the growing awareness and initiatives to mitigate CV health disparities, the data outlined here suggest that more work lies ahead to ensure equitable access and outcomes in the CV device space.

In 2021, the HHS Office of Minority Health and CDC created the Minority Health Social Vulnerability Index (MHSVI), a composite measure designed to assess the needs of communities most susceptible to COVID-19 and facilitate targeted vaccination initiatives in these areas (83). This initiative directly acknowledged the disproportionate impact of COVID-19 on socially high-risk communities, reflected in higher rates of incidence, hospitalization, and mortality. A similar approach is warranted for CV devices to enable more equitable access to innovative, life-saving CV technologies for those most in need.

# Down Syndrome and Quality of Life: A Case Report

Hilary L. Schroeder,1 Marianinha Joanes,2 Raghu Maramraj,3 Andre Small.1

Abstract Background: Quality of life is considered a crucial component to the well-being of patients with Down syndrome. The strength of quality care through stable social and psychological interactions has built a framework for a positive well-being for patients with Down syndrome, improving their quality of life. Case: A 55-year-old African American female with a history of Down syndrome, congenital heart disease, and newly-diagnosed early onset Alzheimer’s disease presented with an arm contusion resulting from regular caretaking. The patient’s history was reviewed, and the complexity of her condition was discovered. While a subset of Down syndrome patients have cardiac complications and others have early-onset Alzheimer’s, our patient had both. We believe this complicated her condition. After the diagnosis of Alzheimer’s was made, the caregivers noticed a significant decline in her ability to communicate and continue day-to-day activities. Despite the decline in functions, a positive mood was apparent. Conclusion: Multiple medical interventions, along with strong family support, positively contri­ buted to the patient’s quality of life. Therapies targeting cognition could result in the maintenance of quality of life and, ultimately, lower health care costs.

Keywords: Down Syndrome; Alzheimer Disease, Early Onset; Heart Defects, Congenital; Quality of Life (Source: MeSH, NLM).

About the Author: Dr. Hilary Schroeder graduated re­ cently from the American University of Antigua in St. John’s, Antigua, West Indies. She is currently completing her first year of Family Medicine residency at the Institute for Family Health in Kingston, New York.

Introduction Quality of life is considered a crucial component to the well-being of patients with Down syndrome. Down syn­ drome treatment should include quality of life improve­ ment measures because although an increase in longevity may not be observed, maintained communication and so­ cial interactions can.1 The strength of quality care through stable social and psychological interactions has built a framework for a positive well-being for people living with disabilities.2 Quality of life is increasingly being recogni­ zed as a measuring tool to assess the progression of di­ sease.3 Within the definition, quality of life encompasses the overall environment and includes the families and friends of Down syndrome patients who provide the hi­ ghest degree of care. Through lifestyle modifications, me­ dical interventions and strong support networks, patients with Down syndrome can increase their life expectancy.4 In this paper, we demonstrate how quality of life is impor­ tant to Down syndrome patients and why quality of life is an important measurement in treating these patients.

The Case Our patient was a 55-year-old African-American female brou­ ght into the Emergency Room by her father (primary caregiver who gave informed consent for this report) in September 2012 with concerns about a large contusion on her arm from routine caregiving. Her past medical history included Down syndrome (1961), mitral valve dysfunction (family could not recall time of diagnosis), and cerebrovascular accident (2010). Patient had no known allergies. Medications included: miconazole (Monis­ tat), warfarin (Coumadin), pantoprazole (Protonix), zinc oxide, phenytoin (Dilantin), protamine sulfate, digoxin (Digox), and acetaminophen (Tylenol). The patient’s father was alive and well at 79 years old, while her mother was 24 years old when birthing her and died at 43 years old from metastatic breast cancer. The patient’s paternal grandmother had Alzheimer’s disease. The patient lived with her father and sister (another caregiver giving informed con­ sent). She was born overseas, had never been employed, but did attend sheltered workshops. She thoroughly enjoyed regu­ larly attending church. Her family denied any alcohol, tobacco, or illicit drug use.

During a home visit in October 2012, we observed our patient, who was bed-bound and unable to communicate her needs effectively, receive exceptional family care. The patient had 24-hour care by her father and daily visits by her sister and a nurse supplied by the hospital. Her father and sister were vigilant about tending to her and ensuring that she try and at least maintain her new skills. They ensured prompt organization of appointments for her cardiac surgeries and follow-up appointments at the hospital and with our team.

Discussion Family Care and Deinstitutionalization Quality of life can be deemed as subjective; however, it is in­ creasingly being recognized as an asset in the monitoring of disease progression.5 Strong family support, solid communi­ cation, and long-lasting friendships have all contributed to in­ creasing the quality of care for patients with Down syndrome. Continuous support and attentiveness by the patient’s father and sister allowed the patient to be interactive and learn new tasks. They carefully monitored her, yet allowed her to practice independence by interacting with the people in her commu­ nity and attending church. This added to her quality of life. Time spent with her family provided us insights on her ability to properly communicate with caregivers and their ability to appropriately interpret her requests. A positive environment empowers Down syndrome patients to continue to learn and teach themselves small tasks in their daily lives.6 External fac­ tors such as socioeconomic factors, strong community support,

and proper daily resources all influence the overall well-being of patients with Down syndrome and increase their ability to function to their maximum capacity.7 Quality of life involves family, environmental and emotional support.

Strengths and Limitations to Our Approach For six months, our group made multiple home visits and in­ teracted with the caregivers to better understand her changing medical status. Over time, it was clear her condition was beco­ ming more complex. As her cognition declined, we relied more on the caregiver’s interpretation of her feelings. Throughout the six-month follow-up period, we maintained constant communi­ cation, tracked patient’s progression, and witnessed the impor­ tance of a positive environment and family support. Historical data gathering was limited by incomplete hospital charts, lack of verbal communication by the patient, and difficulties with data recall by the family.

Conclusion It is our belief that a combination of advanced medical in­ terventions and support greatly improve the quality of life in Down syndrome patients. Treatment of comorbidities, thera­ pies targeting cognition, and added support for patients with Down syndrome help increase their involvement in daily activi­ ties, social bonding, and quality of life.
